e.meaning: good or righteous man (varies with the kanji)
e.etymology: A Japanese men's name whose sense depends on the characters chosen: yoshi may be written as good, righteous, fragrant or joyful, and o as man, husband or hero.
An English surname that began as a medieval nickname for a bald man, from Middle English balled, bald, with the ending -ard.
A spelling of Theodore with the first o dropped. Theodore is from Greek Theodoros, which joins theos (god) and doron (gift).
An American spelling of the German surname Huber, a farmer who held a hide of land. It appeared as a first name around the 1928 election of President Herbert Hoover.

assoc.t: Hoover Dam on the Colorado River
J. Edgar Hoover, longtime FBI director

e.note: Shared with a vacuum cleaner brand; in British English to hoover means to vacuum.

e.etymology: From Hebrew Chuldah, weasel or mole. Huldah is the prophetess King Josiah consults in the Books of Kings. The Scandinavian name Hulda has a separate Old Norse source.
A surname used as a first name, mostly in the South. In Georgia it followed Hoke Smith, governor and senator in the early 1900s, whose middle name was his mother's maiden name.
namesakes: Hoke Colburn (Morgan Freeman's chauffeur in Driving Miss Daisy)

e.etymology: An English surname from the Northamptonshire village of Isham, the name of the River Ise plus Old English ham, homestead.
Its American peak in 1904 followed the hit 1903 song Anona, about an Arizona Indian maiden. The name is also found in Wales, and has been linked to the Latin name Nona, ninth.
Best known from the American modernist writer Djuna Barnes (1892-1982), author of Nightwood, whose unusual name was coined within her own family.
The naval rank used as a first name. Its American peak in 1898 followed Admiral George Dewey's victory at Manila Bay. The word comes through French from Arabic amir, commander.
Several unrelated sources share this spelling: a romanization of Chinese given names and surnames, a variant of Singh, from Sanskrit simha, lion, and an English surname.
An African-American name of the 1970s made by adding the La- prefix to Tasha, the short form of Natasha. Natasha is the Russian pet form of Natalia, from Latin for the Lord's birthday.
A short form of names that begin with D, from Dennis and Dean to Deborah and Diane, given as a full name to both boys and girls since the 1800s.
namesakes: Dee Wallace (actress, the mother in E.T.)

e.etymology: A pet form of Florence and of Flora. Florence comes from Latin florens, flowering or flourishing; Flora is the Roman goddess of flowers.
An African-American name of the 1970s, a variant of Latonia that reads as the La- prefix on Tonya, itself a short form of Antonia.
A spelling of Terry, the pet form of Teresa. Teresa is first recorded for a fourth-century Spanish saint and is of obscure origin; one theory ties it to the Greek island of Thera.
The short form of Bartholomew, from Aramaic bar Talmai, son of Talmai, the name of one of the twelve apostles.
namesakes: Bart Starr (Hall of Fame Packers quarterback)

assoc.t: Bart Simpson, troublemaking son on The Simpsons

e.etymology: Used as a short form of Melvina and as a feminine counterpart to Melvin, mostly in the early and middle 1900s.
An American spelling of Cherie or Sherry with the stress moved to the second syllable. Cherie is French for darling.
An African-American coinage that adds the La- prefix to Wanda.
namesakes: LaWanda Page (Aunt Esther on Sanford and Son)

e.etymology: In the US a spelling of Colleen, from Irish cailin, girl, a name used far more in America and Australia than in Ireland. The same spelling is also recorded as a variant of Coline, from Nicoline.
In the US Marva is usually taken as a feminine form of Marvin; it rose in the mid-1930s, when the boxer Joe Louis married Marva Trotter. It is also an English spelling of the Arabic name Marwa.
An English surname, generally a form of Welburn, from northern English places named for a stream fed by a spring. As a first name it sat alongside Wilbur and Wilbert.
Recorded as a short form of Adelma and of the Irish name Fidelma. In the US around 1900 it also sat easily beside Della, Elma and Velma.
A variant of Maureen, the English form of Irish Mairin, a diminutive of Maire, the Irish Mary.
An American form of Laurine and Lorene, which extend Laura and Lora with the -ine ending. Laura goes back to Latin laurus, the laurel tree.
A feminine spelling of Kerry, from the Irish county and the surname O Ciardha, both built on Irish ciar, black or dark.
Of unclear origin. Its American peak in 1884 matches the presidential campaign of Belva Lockwood, the lawyer and suffragist who ran that year.
From Latin columbus, dove. American parents of the 1800s used it in honor of Christopher Columbus, whose surname is the Latin form of Italian Colombo.
A spelling of Candy, the pet form of Candace. Kandake was the title of the queens of ancient Kush, in what is now Sudan, and appears in the Book of Acts as if it were a name.
e.note: Sounds exactly like the word candy.

assoc.t: candy, the word for sweets (same sound)
